title: Ang 1377–1380: Farid's saloks, first half
hookLine: look under your own collar; dry bread and cool water
tomorrow: Farid says every heart is something precious. what, exactly?

lines: HOW DID A SUFI GET HERE?
cards: The comments under somebody's post are already piling up, and every one is about what that person did wrong. Farid has a couplet for the people typing.
In paraphrase, on ang 1378: Farid, if you're sharp of mind, don't write black marks against anyone; bow your head and look under your own collar. Farid was a Sufi, a Muslim saint of Punjab.
So how did a Sufi's couplets end up in the Sikh scripture?

teach.b: Sikh tradition tells it this way. Guru Nanak, on his travels, came to the place where Farid's line of Sufi teachers lived on, and met the sheikh who kept Farid's words.
Tradition says the verses traveled with the Guru from there, and in time they reached the Granth. The Granth itself doesn't tell the story. It simply gives Farid his own pages, under his own name.
Another, in paraphrase: eat your dry bread and drink cool water; don't look at someone else's buttered bread and burn with wanting.

teach.h: STRUCK? GO HOME, KISS THEIR FEET.
teach.b: And another: if someone strikes you with fists, don't strike back; go home, and kiss their feet. Hard lines, plainly put.
They read like a man talking to himself first, and that's the collar couplet at work: before Farid writes anyone else's black marks, he looks at his own.
The Gurus kept his voice whole. A Muslim saint's words sit in the Sikh scripture beside the Gurus' own, read and sung with the same respect.

how: Farid's saloks are read in the closing pages of the Granth and sung in kirtan like the Gurus' hymns; Sikhs know him as Baba Farid or Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab.

o: where Kabir finds the Lord in forgiveness
Farid begins: look under your own collar
where Guru Arjan's verses of praise begin

p: a Sufi, a Muslim saint of Punjab

s: the Granth holds only the words of the Sikh Gurus
it holds the Bhagats too, among them Farid, a Muslim Sufi, under his own name.
Farid's couplet says don't write black marks against others
bow your head and look under your own collar.
the Granth tells the story of how Farid's verses reached it
that comes from Sikh tradition; the Granth simply gives Farid his pages.

games.q: your group project flopped, and the chat is blaming the one kid who missed a deadline. you missed one too, a smaller one. what does Farid's collar couplet point to?
o: name your own miss first, then talk about fixing it together.
stay quiet; your miss was smaller, so it doesn't really count.
take the blame for all of it so nobody else has to feel bad.
games.why: Farid looks under his own collar before writing anyone else's black marks. that isn't taking all the blame; it's starting with your own part.

practice: If there's water near you, take one slow sip and notice how plain it is: cool, clear, enough. Hold the cup through the sit. Farid's dry bread and cool water are a picture of what's already enough.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1377. Where Farid's couplets begin: look under your own collar before marking anyone else.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Farid, the Sufi whose saloks begin on ang 1377.

carryVoice: Carry this: Farid's couplets, with plain bread, cool water, and your own collar first. Until tomorrow.
